# Four-level distinction table

| Level | Question | Paper commitment | Non-commitment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ontology | What, if anything, is physically fundamental? | Several metaphysical readings are compatible with certified cross-representation invariance. | The formal calculus does not entail ontic structural realism or an information ontology. |
| Semantics | What do variables and models represent? | Meaning is fixed by physical observables, state pairings, redundancies, domains, and interpretation maps. | Coordinate or gauge variables are not automatically physical magnitudes. |
| Epistemology | When is a cross-description claim warranted? | Warrant requires property-relative fidelity, recovery, and uniformity certificates. | Agreement on a restricted observable class is not global equivalence. |
| Proof methodology | What must a derivation explicitly discharge? | Every interface records preserved, approximated, forgotten, and theorem-recovered structure. | A suggestive diagram or shared perturbation series is not a proof object. |

The ontology section is conditional on the semantic and epistemic work.  The
formal results operate at the proof-methodological level and remain useful to
structural realists, entity realists, empiricists, and pragmatists.
